name: Garnet
tagline: A family of deep-red silicate gems
description: Garnet is not a single mineral but a group of closely related silicate minerals — such as almandine, pyrope, spessartine, grossular, andradite and uvarovite — that share the same crystal structure. Garnets most often appear as deep red stones, but the group spans almost every colour. They form mainly in metamorphic rocks and commonly grow as rounded dodecahedral or trapezohedral crystals. Besides jewellery, garnet is widely used as an industrial abrasive.
chemical_formula: X₃Y₂(SiO₄)₃ — general formula of the group
traditional_meanings: Garnet is the traditional birthstone for January. In modern crystal lore it is associated with energy, passion and protection, and historically it was carried by travellers as a protective talisman. These are cultural beliefs, not scientific properties.
care_instructions: Clean with warm, soapy water and a soft brush. Avoid sudden temperature changes and steam cleaning; ultrasonic cleaning is best avoided for stones with fractures or fillings.

name: Goldstone
description: Goldstone is a glittering glass made by melting silica with copper compounds under carefully controlled, oxygen-poor conditions so that countless tiny copper crystals form inside the glass and sparkle in light (an effect called aventurescence). It is not a natural mineral, although it is often sold alongside crystals. Blue goldstone gets its colour from cobalt; green goldstone from chromium. Popular stories credit 17th-century Venetian glassmakers with its invention.
chemical_formula: Silica glass containing small copper crystals (cobalt or chromium in blue/green types)
sources: Produced today in several countries including Italy, China and India
traditional_meanings: In modern crystal lore goldstone is called a "stone of ambition" and is associated with confidence and optimism. These are cultural beliefs; goldstone itself is a man-made material.
care_instructions: Clean with mild soap and water and dry with a soft cloth. Avoid hard knocks and harsh chemicals — like any glass it can chip or scratch.

name: Hematite
tagline: Metallic iron oxide with a blood-red streak
description: Hematite is an iron oxide and the most important ore of iron. Polished hematite looks silvery-grey and almost mirror-like, yet it leaves a reddish-brown streak when rubbed on unglazed porcelain — the origin of its name, from the Greek word for blood. Powdered hematite (red ochre) has been used as a pigment since prehistoric times. Note that much of the strongly magnetic "hematite" sold as jewellery is actually a man-made material.

characteristics.Magnetism: Natural hematite is at most weakly magnetic

traditional_meanings: In modern crystal lore hematite is considered a grounding and protective stone. These are cultural beliefs, not scientific properties.
care_instructions: Wipe with a soft, dry or slightly damp cloth and dry immediately. Avoid long soaking and salt water, which can cause rust spots, and store away from harder stones to prevent scratches.

name: Herkimer Diamond
description: Herkimer diamonds are not diamonds: they are exceptionally clear, naturally double-terminated quartz crystals found in cavities of Cambrian-age dolostone around Herkimer County and the Mohawk River Valley in New York, USA. Their bright natural facets form during growth, without any cutting, which gives them a diamond-like sparkle. Some contain tiny black inclusions of hydrocarbon material.
sources: Herkimer County and the Mohawk River Valley, New York, USA (the classic locality)
Similar double-terminated quartz from other countries is sometimes sold under this name
traditional_meanings: In modern crystal lore Herkimer diamonds are called "stones of attunement" and are believed to amplify energy and dreams. These are cultural beliefs, not scientific properties.
care_instructions: Rinse in lukewarm water with mild soap and dry with a soft cloth. Quartz is hard, but the delicate points can chip — store separately.

name: Lapis Lazuli
description: Lapis lazuli is a metamorphic rock, not a single mineral. Its intense blue comes mainly from the mineral lazurite, often accompanied by white calcite and golden flecks of pyrite. It has been mined in the mountains of north-eastern Afghanistan for thousands of years, was used in ancient Egyptian and Mesopotamian jewellery, and was ground to make the pigment ultramarine prized by Renaissance painters.
mineral_family: Rock composed mainly of lazurite, with calcite, pyrite and other minerals
chemical_formula: Variable (rock); main mineral lazurite is a sulfur-bearing sodium-calcium aluminosilicate

characteristics.Typical features: Gold pyrite flecks and white calcite veining

traditional_meanings: Lapis lazuli has long been associated with royalty, wisdom and truth, and in modern crystal lore it is linked to the throat and third-eye chakras. These are cultural beliefs, not scientific properties.
care_instructions: Lapis is fairly soft and porous: clean only with a soft, dry or barely damp cloth. Avoid ultrasonic and steam cleaners, acids, perfumes and long soaking.

name: Libyan Desert Glass
tagline: Ancient natural glass from the Sahara
description: Libyan Desert Glass is a rare, nearly pure silica glass found scattered across parts of the Great Sand Sea in western Egypt, near the Libyan border. It formed about 29 million years ago from intense heat — most researchers link it to a meteorite impact or airburst. A carved piece of this glass forms the central scarab of a pectoral found in the tomb of Tutankhamun.
mineral_family: Natural silica glass (impact-related; origin still studied)

characteristics.Typical features: Wind-sculpted surfaces, bubbles and dark streaks

sources: Great Sand Sea, western Egypt (near the Libyan border)
traditional_meanings: In modern crystal lore it is regarded as a stone of manifestation and solar energy. These are cultural beliefs, not scientific properties.
care_instructions: Clean with water and a soft cloth. It is brittle — avoid knocks and sudden temperature changes.

name: Obsidian
description: Obsidian is natural volcanic glass that forms when silica-rich lava cools too quickly for crystals to grow. It breaks with a smooth, curved (conchoidal) fracture that produces extremely sharp edges, so it was used for blades, arrowheads and mirrors by many ancient cultures. Varieties include snowflake obsidian (white cristobalite spots), mahogany obsidian and rainbow or sheen obsidian.
traditional_meanings: In modern crystal lore obsidian is considered a protective, grounding stone; polished obsidian mirrors were used in Mesoamerica. These are cultural beliefs and practices, not scientific properties.
care_instructions: Clean with mild soap and water. It is brittle and edges can be sharp — handle carefully and avoid impacts.

name: Red Beryl
tagline: One of the rarest gemstones on Earth
description: Red beryl is a rare red variety of the mineral beryl, the same species as emerald and aquamarine. Its colour comes from traces of manganese. It was first described from Utah in 1904, and gem-quality crystals have been mined commercially only in the Wah Wah Mountains of Utah, USA. Crystals are usually small and often contain inclusions and fractures. The trade name "bixbite" is discouraged because it is easily confused with the mineral bixbyite.
sources: Minor occurrences in New Mexico, USA
traditional_meanings: Because it was only discovered in 1904, red beryl has little historical lore; modern crystal sellers associate it with vitality and passion. These are cultural beliefs, not scientific properties.
care_instructions: Usually fractured and often clarity-enhanced: clean only with warm, soapy water and a soft brush. Avoid ultrasonic and steam cleaners.

name: Red Jasper
description: Jasper is an opaque, fine-grained variety of quartz (often grouped with chalcedony) that can contain a significant proportion of other materials. Red jasper owes its brick-red colour to iron oxides, mainly hematite. It takes a good polish and has been carved into seals, beads and ornaments since ancient times.
traditional_meanings: In modern crystal lore red jasper is called a "stone of endurance" and is associated with stability and the root chakra. These are cultural beliefs, not scientific properties.
care_instructions: Clean with warm, soapy water and a soft brush. Durable for everyday wear; avoid harsh chemicals.

name: Rose Quartz
description: Rose quartz is a pale to medium pink variety of quartz. It usually occurs in massive, translucent and somewhat cloudy form; well-formed rose quartz crystals are rare. Research attributes its colour to microscopic fibrous inclusions of a mineral related to dumortierite. Strong, prolonged sunlight can slowly fade the colour.
traditional_meanings: Rose quartz is widely called the "stone of love" in crystal lore and is associated with compassion and the heart chakra. These are cultural beliefs, not scientific properties.
care_instructions: Clean with mild soap and water. Keep out of prolonged direct sunlight to avoid fading.

name: Shungite
description: Shungite is a black, non-crystalline, carbon-rich rock from the Karelia region of north-western Russia, named after the village of Shunga near Lake Onega. It is about two billion years old. The shiny, high-carbon variety is sometimes sold as "elite" or "noble" shungite. Popular claims that shungite blocks phone radiation or purifies the body are not supported by scientific evidence.
chemical_formula: Mostly carbon (C), with silicate minerals; carbon content varies widely

characteristics.Other: Conducts electricity; can leave black marks

sources: Karelia, Russia (Lake Onega region, near Shunga)
traditional_meanings: Shungite is popular in modern wellness culture for "purifying" water and energy. These are beliefs, not established scientific properties.
care_instructions: Relatively soft and can leave black marks: wipe with a dry cloth. If rinsed, dry it immediately.

name: Smoky Quartz
tagline: Brown to black quartz coloured by natural radiation
description: Smoky quartz is a translucent grey-brown to almost black variety of quartz. Its colour develops when natural radiation from surrounding rocks acts on traces of aluminium in the crystal; heating can lighten or remove the colour. Some smoky quartz on the market is colourless quartz that has been artificially irradiated. It is regarded as the national gem of Scotland, where it is known as cairngorm.
traditional_meanings: In modern crystal lore smoky quartz is associated with grounding and calm. It is also set into traditional Scottish jewellery. These are cultural beliefs and traditions, not scientific properties.
care_instructions: Clean with mild soap and water. Avoid heat and long exposure to strong sunlight, which can lighten the colour.

name: Tiger's Eye
tagline: Golden quartz with a silky moving shine
description: Tiger's eye is a chatoyant variety of quartz: when polished into a dome it shows a silky band of light that moves as the stone is turned, like a cat's eye. The effect comes from a fibrous structure formed where quartz developed together with, and replaced, fibres of the blue asbestiform mineral crocidolite (riebeckite) that later altered to iron oxides, giving the golden-brown colour. The blue-grey variety is called hawk's eye.
traditional_meanings: In modern crystal lore tiger's eye is associated with courage, focus and protection. These are cultural beliefs, not scientific properties.
care_instructions: Clean with warm, soapy water and a soft cloth. Avoid long soaking and harsh chemicals.
